extracted.intended_audience: advanced undergraduate / beginning graduate students and researchers studying first-order logic and model theory; readers of a mathematical logic textbook
extracted.subtask_description: Exposition of decidability, model-size results, theories and axiomatizability, categoricity tests, prenex normal form, and definitions/interpretations in first-order logic. Contains theorems, proofs, examples, and algorithmic observations about finite structures and theories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Finite-structure specification by a finite string
rubrics_metrics.description: A finite structure for a finite language can be specified by a finite string of symbols (e.g., listing the universe {1,...,n} and the relations as tuples).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such a specification can be written with numerals and punctuation and thus communicated to a person or machine; the finite string can be written in a suitable input format. (Example given: ({1,2,3,4}; {⟨1,2⟩,⟨2,1⟩,⟨2,3⟩,⟨3,3⟩}).)

rubrics_metrics.name: Decidability of satisfaction in a given finite structure
rubrics_metrics.description: Given a finite structure A with universe {1,...,n}, a wff ϕ, and an assignment sϕ of numbers to the free variables, we can effectively decide whether |=A ϕ[sϕ].
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluation can be organized as a computation tree where each quantifier triggers a search through the n-element universe; for a formula with k quantifiers the number of leaves is bounded by a polynomial in n of degree k. If the language has function symbols, each term is evaluated using the finite function of the structure. This yields an effective decision procedure for satisfaction in finite structures (even for sentences).

rubrics_metrics.name: Theorem 26C: Th A is decidable for finite A
rubrics_metrics.description: For a finite structure A in a finite language, Th A (the set of all sentences true in A) is decidable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Two proofs given: (1) replace A by an isomorphic structure with universe {1,...,n} and use effective satisfaction testing; (2) form a sentence δA that specifies A up to isomorphism and observe Th A = {σ | δA |= σ }, then apply enumerability/decidability results. Either way, membership in Th A can be decided.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decidability of existence of an n-element model for a sentence
rubrics_metrics.description: Given a sentence σ and a positive integer n, one can effectively decide whether σ has an n-element model.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: By observation 1 every n-element model can be represented with universe {1,...,n}; with the language restricted to symbols in σ there are only finitely many such structures (e.g., for a single binary predicate there are 2^{n^2} possibilities). Systematically generate all these structures and test each for satisfaction using the finite-structure satisfaction procedure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spectrum of a sentence is decidable
rubrics_metrics.description: The spectrum { n | σ has a model of size n } of any sentence σ is a decidable set of positive integers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follows from the effective decidability of whether σ has an n-element model for each n.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theorem 26D: sentences with finite models are effectively enumerable
rubrics_metrics.description: For a finite language, the set {σ | σ has a finite model} is effectively enumerable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Semidecision procedure: given σ, check for a model of size 1, then 2, then 3, ... using the decidability for fixed sizes; if σ has any finite model this search will eventually find one.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corollary 26E: complement of sentences true in every finite structure is enumerable
rubrics_metrics.description: Let F be the set of sentences true in every finite structure. Then the complement of F is effectively enumerable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: σ ∈ F^c iff (¬σ) has a finite model; apply the semidecision procedure enumerating finite models to (¬σ).

rubrics_metrics.name: Trakhtenbrot’s theorem (negative result)
rubrics_metrics.description: The set of sentences true in every finite structure is, in general, not decidable or effectively enumerable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shows failure of the finite-structure analogue of enumerability theorems (stated without proof).

rubrics_metrics.name: Countability of constructed Henkin-style models
rubrics_metrics.description: If the initial language is countable, then the canonical model A/E constructed in the completeness proof has countable universe (so a consistent set of sentences in a countable language has a countable model).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The preliminary structure A is the set of all terms in a countable augmented language (countable), and A/E is a set of equivalence classes injectively mapped into A, hence countable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Löwenheim–Skolem theorem (downward and cardinality ≤λ version)
rubrics_metrics.description: (a) If a set of formulas in a countable language is satisfiable then it is satisfiable in some countable structure. (b) If a set of sentences in a countable language has any model, it has a countable model. More generally: if the language has cardinality λ, then any satisfiable set has a model of cardinality ≤ λ; any set of sentences with a model has a model of cardinality ≤ λ.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof outline: completeness/constructive model gives A/E of cardinality ≤ λ. The ℵ0-case is the classical Löwenheim–Skolem; the more general statement follows by counting terms in a language of size λ. Consequence: noncategoricity of theories with infinite models in first-order logic (they admit multiple cardinalities).

rubrics_metrics.name: LST upward Löwenheim–Skolem theorem
rubrics_metrics.description: If a set of formulas in a language of cardinality λ is satisfiable in some infinite structure, then for every cardinal κ ≥ λ there is a structure of cardinality κ in which the set is satisfiable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construct by expanding the language with κ new constant symbols, force them to be distinct, apply compactness to get a model, then restrict to the original language. Corollaries: if a theory has any infinite model it has models of every infinite cardinality (for countable languages).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of theory and Th K
rubrics_metrics.description: A theory is a set of sentences closed under logical implication: T is a theory iff whenever T |= σ then σ ∈ T. For a class K of structures, Th K = {σ | σ is true in every member of K}.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Th K is the set of consequences of K; for T = Th K this closure property holds. Examples: Th of class of fields, etc.

rubrics_metrics.name: Completeness of a theory
rubrics_metrics.description: A theory T is complete iff for every sentence σ, either σ ∈ T or (¬σ) ∈ T.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Th A for a single structure A is always complete. Equivalently, a theory is complete iff any two models of T are elementarily equivalent. Theories like 'fields' are not complete because some sentences distinguish fields of different properties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Axiomatizable and finitely axiomatizable theories
rubrics_metrics.description: T is axiomatizable iff there is a decidable set Σ of sentences with T = Cn(Σ). T is finitely axiomatizable iff T = Cn(Σ) for some finite Σ (equivalently T = Cn{σ} for a single conjunction σ).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: theory of fields is finitely axiomatizable; theory of fields of characteristic 0 is axiomatizable but not finitely axiomatizable (needs infinitely many sentences stating 1+...+1 ≠ 0). Theorem 26H: if Cn(Σ) is finitely axiomatizable then there is a finite Σ0 ⊆ Σ with same consequences (compactness argument).

rubrics_metrics.name: Corollary 26I: enumerability and decidability consequences
rubrics_metrics.description: (a) An axiomatizable theory (in a reasonable language) is effectively enumerable. (b) A complete axiomatizable theory (in a reasonable language) is decidable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use effective enumerability of axioms plus completeness to decide membership in the theory (search enumerated consequences until either σ or ¬σ appears).

rubrics_metrics.name: Łoś–Vaught test for completeness
rubrics_metrics.description: Let T be a theory in a countable language with no finite models. (a) If T is ℵ0-categorical (all infinite countable models are isomorphic) then T is complete. (b) If T is κ-categorical for some infinite cardinal κ (and the language cardinality ≤ κ), then T is complete.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof uses upward/downward Löwenheim–Skolem and categoricity to show any two models are elementarily equivalent. Note the converse is false: some complete theories are not κ-categorical for any κ.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examples: completeness and decidability of algebraically closed fields and complex field
rubrics_metrics.description: (a) The theory of algebraically closed fields of characteristic 0 is complete. (b) The theory of the complex field C = (C;0,1,+,·) is decidable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Axiomatize algebraically closed fields of characteristic 0 by field axioms plus sentences asserting existence of roots for polynomials; this set is decidable and axiomatizes the class, and by Łoś–Vaught (using categoricity in uncountable cardinals via algebraic facts like Steinitz theorem) the theory is complete, hence decidable. The real field's decidability is noted as a deeper result (Tarski).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prenex Normal Form theorem
rubrics_metrics.description: Every formula is logically equivalent to a prenex formula (a string of quantifiers Q1 x1 ... Qn xn followed by a quantifier-free formula).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quantifier manipulation rules given (Q1a/b, Q2a/b, Q3a/b) such as ¬∀x α ≡ ∃x ¬α and moving quantifiers across implications when variable conditions hold. Inductive construction: atomic formulas are already prenex; use rules to move quantifiers outward for ¬, ∀, and → cases. Examples show latitude in ordering quantifiers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Goodness condition for definitions of function symbols (well-definedness)
rubrics_metrics.description: When adding a defined function symbol f by the sentence δ: ∀v1 ∀v2[ f v1 = v2 ↔ ϕ(v1,v2) ], the definition is 'noncreative' (does not add new consequences in the original language) iff T proves the uniqueness/existence condition ∀v1 ∃!v2 ϕ(v1,v2).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Theorem 27A: (a) noncreative definition: for any sentence σ in the smaller language, T;δ |= σ implies T |= σ. (b) equivalent condition: ε := ∀v1 ∃!v2 ϕ is in the theory T. Example of bad definition given (f(x)=y iff x<y) which fails uniqueness and yields contradictions. Proof constructs from T |= ε a function F in each model A to expand A to (A,F) satisfying δ and preserving original-language sentences.
